name: Nanjing
info: Nanjing is a city on the lower Yangtze in Jiangsu province, China, which served as the capital of Eastern Wu, the Eastern Jin and Southern dynasties, the Southern Tang, the early Ming and the Republic of China.

facts.founded: Historical records attribute the first named urban foundations in the area to the 5th century BCE, Yuecheng and Yecheng, though their locations and dates are debated; Sun Quan moved his headquarters to Moling in 211 and built the Stone City, and made it his capital in 229.
facts.where: On the lower Yangtze River in the Yangtze River Delta, in the south-western corner of Jiangsu province, China, with the Qinhuai River running through the main urban area and the Ningzheng Ridge round its north, east and south sides.
facts.known: Capital of Eastern Wu, the Eastern Jin, the Southern dynasties, the Southern Tang, the early Ming and the Republic of China; Jiankang's Buddhist monasteries; the Ming city wall and Xiaoling mausoleum; the Taiping capital Tianjing; the Treaty of Nanking; the Nanjing Massacre of 1937–1938
facts.today: Nanjing is the capital of Jiangsu province and a sub-provincial city of the People's Republic of China, with about 9.4 million people.

t: Under the names Jianye, Jiankang, Jiangning and Nanjing, the city was the seat of many regimes from the 3rd century CE, among them Eastern Wu, the Eastern Jin and Southern dynasties, the Southern Tang, the early Ming and the Republic of China.

It was destroyed or plundered several times: by the Sui in 589, by the Northern Song in 976, by the Qing in 1864 after the fall of the Taiping capital, and by the Japanese army in 1937, when the Nanjing Massacre began.
When the Yongle Emperor moved the Ming capital to Beijing in 1421 Nanjing became a secondary capital, and it grew into a commercial and cultural city of silk, publishing and examinations.
dyk: The Sultan of Boni died during a state visit to the Ming capital in 1408 and was buried in Nanjing, where the Interpreters Institute housed foreign envoys.
ev: Sun Quan proclaims himself emperor and makes Jianye the capital of Eastern Wu
Sima Rui makes Jiankang his capital, and the Eastern Jin dynasty follows
Emperor Wen of Sui orders Jiankang demolished
Xu Zhigao becomes emperor of the Southern Tang, with Jiangning as capital
Zhu Yuanzhang takes the throne as the Hongwu Emperor and names the city Nanjing
Taiping forces capture the city and make it their capital, Tianjing
The Kuomintang National Government declares Nanjing the national capital
Japanese forces take the city on 13 December and the Nanjing Massacre begins

sections.origins:
Human habitation in the Nanjing region dates to the Neolithic period. The type-site of the Beiyinyangying culture, near the modern urban core, contains a cemetery with 225 burials and grave goods such as polished stone tools, jade and agate, which indicate connections with the Lake Tai region. The Bronze Age Hushu culture characterised the Nanjing–Zhenjiang area in the second millennium BCE, and at the Xijie site on the south bank of the Qinhuai River excavations have identified a fortified settlement with concentric ditches and wall foundations from the Shang–Zhou transition. Its relationship to later cities is undetermined.

Historical records attribute the first named urban foundations in the area to the 5th century BCE: Yuecheng, reportedly built by Fan Li of Yue, and Yecheng, attributed to King Fuchai of Wu. Their exact locations and dates remain debated. Under Chu rule the area was known as Jinling, and after the Qin unification it was renamed Moling. The site lies where the Yangtze flows past the west and then the north side of the city, and the Qinhuai River runs from south to north through the main urban area to join it.
sections.growth:
In 211 Sun Quan moved his headquarters to Moling, and the next year he fortified Shitou Hill to build the Stone City and renamed the region Jianye. After he proclaimed himself emperor in 229 he established his capital there. Under the Eastern Jin the city was Jiankang, and a rebuilding between 330 and 332 defined its layout for the Southern Dynasties. Canals connected it to regional centres, and commerce centred on four large walled markets plus smaller specialised ones. By the Liang dynasty it housed over 500 monasteries, and in the first half of the 6th century its population likely exceeded 300,000.

The Ming city had four nested zones: the Forbidden City, the Imperial City, the Capital City and the Outer Enclosure. The Capital City wall exceeded 30 kilometres, and the Outer Enclosure covered approximately 230 square kilometres. By 1391 the permanent population within the Outer Enclosure was estimated at between 900,000 and one million. After the capital moved to Beijing in 1421 the registered population fell to between 200,000 and 300,000, but by the mid-Ming period private silk-weaving, fan-making and commercial publishing flourished, and under the Qing the number of private satin looms was estimated to have exceeded 30,000 at its peak.
sections.rulers:
Nanjing was the capital of Eastern Wu (229–280). After Sima Rui made Jiankang his capital in 317, the Eastern Jin and the Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang and Chen dynasties ruled southern China from it until 589, when Emperor Wen of Sui took the city. For the next three centuries it was a demoted settlement. Xu Zhigao became emperor of the Southern Tang on 11 November 937, with Jiangning as capital, and the Northern Song took it in 976. Under the Southern Song it was a provisional capital for the fleeing court from May 1129 and kept its prestige as a secondary capital until the Mongols took it in 1275.

Zhu Yuanzhang captured the city in 1356 and took the throne there in 1368 as the Hongwu Emperor. Zhu Di seized it in 1402, and in 1421 he moved the capital to Beijing; from 1441 Nanjing was the secondary capital, with a parallel but mainly symbolic set of ministries. The Prince of Fu was enthroned there in June 1644 as the Hongguang Emperor of the Southern Ming, and Dodo's army entered on 6 June 1645. The Qing renamed it Jiangning and made it seat of the Governor-General of Liangjiang. Taiping forces held it from 1853 to 1864.

Sun Yat-sen was sworn in there as provisional president on 1 January 1912, and the government moved to Beijing within weeks. On 1 June 1927 the Kuomintang government declared it the national capital.
sections.life:
Jiankang was a major centre of East Asian Buddhism and of literary life: the region's vernacular lyrics were codified as the Yuefu corpus "Songs of Wu", and circles such as the "Eight Friends of Jingling" met in the late 5th century. Under the Ming the city hosted foreign envoys at the Interpreters Institute, and the Longjiang shipyard built vessels for the Treasure Fleet. In the late 16th century Jesuit missionaries led by Matteo Ricci settled there; friction with the authorities led to the Nanjing Incident of 1616–1617 and the expulsion of several Jesuits to Macao.

In 1649 the Qing built a walled Manchu City in the east, separating the Eight Banner garrison from the Han population's quarter. The Jiangnan examination compound expanded from 7,500 candidates in 1630 to 17,000 by 1850, and Yuan Mei made his Suiyuan garden a home for women disciples. Under the Taiping, residents were segregated by sex into occupational units, and many Buddhist and Taoist temples were destroyed or converted. Missionaries founded Nanking University in 1888 and Drum Tower Hospital in 1892. In the Nanjing Decade the city was home to National Central University, Academia Sinica and the Purple Mountain Observatory, while a 1934 survey found that about 45.1 per cent of households lived in shantytowns.
sections.crises:
The Su Jun Rebellion (327–329) destroyed the imperial palaces. In 548 Hou Jing besieged Taicheng for five months, and in 552 loyalist forces defeated him and looted the city. In 589 the Sui ordered Jiankang demolished, and its walls, palaces and residences were levelled and the land reclaimed for agriculture. In 976, after Northern Song forces besieged the city, Jinling was plundered following Li Yu's surrender, though the Song commander Cao Bin tried to restrain his troops. In March 1853, when Taiping forces captured the city, the Manchu garrison, its families, Qing officials and local militia suffered heavy casualties through combat, suicide and executions by Taiping forces, who called them "Qing demons". When the city fell in July 1864 after a siege, Qing forces engaged in widespread looting, arson and killing, and destroyed large parts of it, including the Taiping palaces.

Japanese troops entered Nanjing on 13 December 1937, the day after General Tang Shengzhi ordered a retreat. Over the following weeks they killed civilians and captured soldiers and raped women and girls, and arson destroyed one third of the city. A committee of foreigners led by John Rabe set up the Nanking Safety Zone, credited with saving at least 200,000 lives. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East estimated more than 200,000 dead and the Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal of 1947 more than 300,000; newer estimates run between 100,000 and 200,000. Japanese nationalists and revisionists have denied or minimised the massacre.
sections.legacy:
The ruins of Jiankang became a frequent subject of classical poetry, and by the late Tang this had developed into a nostalgic tradition called "Meditation on the Past at Jinling". The name Nanjing, "Southern Capital", was formally established in 1368 to distinguish the new capital from the "Northern Capital" at Kaifeng, and it later served as the counterpart to Beijing. A court language widely believed to be derived from Nanjing speech was used under the Ming and Qing until the mid-nineteenth century, but Standard Mandarin was based on Beijing speech, not on that of Nanjing.

The city is recognised as one of the Four Great Ancient Capitals of China. Its heritage sites include the Ming city wall, the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum, the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum and the Presidential Palace, and its museums include the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall and the Taiping Kingdom History Museum. The Treaty of Nanking, which ended the First Opium War, was signed on the British warship HMS Cornwallis at Xiaguan in August 1842.

After 1949 Nanjing was a province-level municipality, and since 1952 it has been the capital of Jiangsu. The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, designed and built by Chinese engineers, was begun in 1960 and opened in 1968. About 9.4 million people live in the city.

summary: Nanjing, on the lower Yangtze, was the capital of Eastern Wu, the Eastern Jin and Southern dynasties, the Southern Tang, the early Ming and the Republic of China. It was sacked or demolished several times, and in 1937 Japanese troops carried out the Nanjing Massacre. It is now the capital of Jiangsu.
references: Jun Fang, China's Second Capital – Nanjing Under the Ming, 1368-1644 (Routledge, 2014)
Edward L. Farmer, Early Ming Government: The Evolution of Dual Capitals (Harvard University Press, 1976)
Albert E. Dien, The Cambridge History of China, Volume 2: The Six Dynasties, 220–589 (Cambridge University Press, 2019)
Albert E. Dien, Six dynasties civilization (Yale University Press, 2007)
notes: START: the article dates no founding. Records attribute Yuecheng and Yecheng to the 5th century BCE with locations and dates debated; I used -500 with circa true. Alternative: 211 (Sun Quan's move) or 229.

REVISION (massacre): the second and third paragraphs of 'crises' were replaced by one paragraph from the Nanjing Massacre article (wp2): the fall on 13 December 1937 (Tang's retreat order on 12 December is in both sources), killing of civilians and captured soldiers, rape, arson destroying one third of the city, the Safety Zone under John Rabe (credited with saving at least 200,000 lives), the tribunals' estimates (IMTFE more than 200,000; Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal 1947 more than 300,000), newer estimates of 100,000 to 200,000, and denial or minimising by Japanese nationalists and revisionists. The earlier sentences on the bombing from 15 August, the move to Chongqing and the USS Panay were dropped to make room. The Safety Zone figure is a credit the article states, not a count.

DISAGREEMENT between sources: the city article says the toll was 'between 300,000 and 350,000' (the earlier draft used this); the Nanjing Massacre article gives the IMTFE as more than 200,000, the 1947 tribunal as more than 300,000, newer estimates 100,000 to 200,000, and others from 40,000 to over 340,000 (the last for the whole Shanghai-Nanjing region). I used the massacre article's figures and left out the city article's range. The massacre article also says 300,000 is the Chinese government's endorsed figure and that some scholars (Hata, Wakabayashi) regard it as symbolic or as covering the whole Yangtze delta; not included for space. The massacre article gives the period as six weeks by traditional dating and says atrocities in the area lasted to late March 1938; I wrote 'following weeks'. The key event for 1937 and the lead takeaways were left as they were.

Names: the article gives Jinling, Moling, Jianye (211/212), Jiankang (313), Jiangning, Shangyuan (761), Jiqing (1329), Yingtian (1356), Tianjing (1853), Nanjing (1368). I used Jianye/Jiankang/Jiangning in the first takeaway as the article gives them; the Tang renaming to Shangyuan and Mongol-era Jiqing are left out for space.

'Southern Song provisional capital from May 1129': the article says Jiankang was renamed and held a provisional court, which Gaozong left three months later for Lin'an, and that it 'retained its prestige as a secondary capital' until 1275. I wrote it as the article does.

The article says the Ming capital period was 1368-1421 in the lead and that Nanjing remained the secondary capital after 1441; 'formally dropped' of Beijing's xingzai prefix in 1441. The 1425 Hongxi attempt is left out.

Early statement: Xu Zhigao 'ascending the throne as emperor of the Southern Tang on November 11 937' is given as 11 November 937; fall 'January 4 976' as 4 January 976 (the article writes 'In early 975 ... besieged', 'on January 4 976 the city fell'; I wrote 976 for the fall).

Capital Plan, Zhongshan Road axis, the 1927 Nanjing Incident (British and American warships bombarding parts of the city), the 1927 April violence, the 1913 sack by Zhang Xun's troops, the 1842 treaty detail and the 21 September air operation warnings were left out for space (1842 treaty included briefly).

Population: 'about 9.4 million' from 9,423,400 in 2021; the 'as of' is dropped as the guide asks. The article's present-day material on economy, ranking, universities and sister cities was left out. The Nagoya sister-city suspension of 2012 after its mayor denied the massacre was left out as present-day politics.
Section lengths: see the checker; the Jiankang population 'likely exceeded 300,000' is the article's hedge. 1391 and post-1421 figures are the article's 'estimated' and 'registered' figures.
The article's 'Amity Printing Company', GDP, climate, transport, culture lists and notable people were not used.
